The Woodchat shrike (Lanius senator) is a medium-sized passerine of the Laniidae family that exhibits a characteristic life-history pattern for a migratory insectivorous bird common in Mediterranean and temperate regions. For eggs incubated under field conditions, the mean incubation temperature has been estimated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and under this thermal regime the embryo completes development and hatches after approximately 15.7 days [ab = approximately 15.7 days]. Newly hatched nestlings emerge with a wet weight at birth of 3.5 grams [Wwb = 3.5 grams], a relatively modest mass that represents only a small fraction of the adult body size and underscores the altricial nature of this species, which depends entirely on biparental provisioning during the early nestling phase. The relatively short incubation period and small hatchling mass are typical of many temperate-latitude passerines and reflect the trade-off between rapid development and the initial energetic investment in the egg.

During the nestling phase, which unfolds under the warmer body temperatures typical of actively brooded chicks at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young birds achieve the ability to leave the nest and sustain flight at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching]. This rapid fledging period is relatively short compared to many other passerines of similar body mass and reflects the selective pressure of a short breeding season in a migratory species that must complete its reproductive cycle before autumn departure. Observations from Mediterranean field sites indicate that the chicks develop quickly, gaining mass steadily as both parents deliver a diet dominated by large insects and small vertebrates. The timing of nest departure is closely linked to the local abundance of prey, and fledglings typically remain near the nest site for several days afterward, still receiving occasional food deliveries from attending adults as they refine their hunting skills.

Following the fledging period and subsequent nutritional independence, young Woodchat shrikes undergo a longer developmental trajectory before they become reproductively competent. Under the same thermal conditions characteristic of active adult metabolism, estimated at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], puberty or sexual maturity is attained at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching]. This relatively early maturation, occurring within the same calendar year as hatching, is consistent with the life cycle of a short-lived migratory passerine that must breed in its first spring to maintain population stability. However, while the gonads mature early, the actual initiation of breeding is deferred until the following breeding season, as young birds must first complete their post-juvenile molt, acquire a territory, and secure a mate. The short interval to reproductive maturation reflects the species' high intrinsic rate of increase and its dependence on high annual fecundity.

First reproduction in Woodchat shrike occurs during the subsequent breeding season, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days] under the typical body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This interval corresponds to a single annual cycle, such that individuals hatched in one spring typically breed for the first time in the following spring, at approximately one year of age. The maximum reproductive rate, when conditions are optimal, reaches 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 5 eggs per clutch], a modest but productive clutch size for a passerine of this body size, typically slightly larger than that of many tropical congeners. This reproductive output, a single annual clutch [F_R_i = a single annual clutch] is sufficient to offset adult mortality in stable populations.

The ultimate adult wet weight of the Woodchat shrike reaches approximately 36 grams [Wwi = approximately 36 grams], a typical body mass for a medium-sized insectivorous passerine. Regarding lifespan, field studies based on ringing and recapture data indicate that the maximum recorded longevity for this species is 5.7 years [am = 5.7 years] when considered under the active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], though most individuals likely survive for considerably shorter periods due to the hazards of migration and winter mortality. This relatively short lifespan, combined with the early age at first reproduction and the moderate clutch size, characterizes a life history strategy adapted to unstable environments where high annual mortality is compensated by high annual fecundity.
